wine.name: Rare Rutherglen Muscat
wine.classification: Rare, the fourth rung, above Grand, of the Muscat of Rutherglen classification
wine.grapes: Brown Muscat alone, the red skinned Muscat à Petits Grains of Rutherglen.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards at Rosewood on the Corowa road just west of the township, where Brown Muscat was replanted on American rootstock from 1901; the house draws on vines planted in those years, by its own account.
wine.making: The grapes hang until they shrivel towards raisins, are pressed and barely fermented before grape spirit stops them, then enter the house's modified solera: a run of small barrels from quarter casks to puncheons, then a cask of about 1,800 litres from which the Rare is drawn and bottled only as needed. The solera was laid down on base wines of the 1890s and 1900, by the house's account.
wine.glass: Deep mahogany, with raisin, coffee grounds, treacle and marzipan over toasted walnut and burnt orange peel; thick and very sweet, warmed by its spirit, with a nutty, rancio edge and a finish that lasts for minutes.
wine.ageing: Ready when bottled, since its age is in the solera rather than the bottle; it changes little with keeping, and an opened bottle lasts for weeks.
wine.serve: Lightly chilled, 10 to 13 degrees Celsius, cooler in warm weather as the house advises; no decanting; a small white wine glass and a small pour.

records.table: From a solera the house says it laid down on wines of the 1890s comes Chambers Rosewood's Rare Rutherglen Muscat: raisined Brown Muscat, fortified and aged for decades in old casks until it tastes of treacle, coffee and walnut. A small glass, lightly chilled, is enough.
records.story: The founder left Norfolk after a quarrel with his employer, by the family's account, and in 1858 planted vines just west of Rutherglen with the help of his sons. A rose hedge set round the boundary gave the property its name, Rosewood. The gold rush had filled the district with miners, and fortified wine was what they drank. Phylloxera struck Rutherglen's vines in 1899, and in 1901 the family began replanting on American rootstock. The founder's grandson, the third generation, laid the foundations of the house's soleras of Muscat and Muscadelle on base wines of the 1890s and 1900, by the house's account, and each generation since has drawn from them and topped them up, so that a bottle of Rare carries a thread of wine older than anyone who drinks it. Bill Chambers (1933 to 2023), the fifth generation, a winemaker and wine judge, returned to Rutherglen in the late 1950s and carried the house through the later twentieth century. The wine agreement Australia signed with the European Union in 2008 phased out the name Tokay, which left Australian labels in 2020, and the house labels that wine by its grape, Muscadelle. A Rutherglen Muscat's age, Chambers shows, lives in the solera and not in a year on the label.

wine.making: Late picked Brown Muscat is fortified with grape spirit and laid down in old oak casks. The Old Premium Rare is blended from very old reserves with younger wines, only the chosen lots of each vintage going in, to an average age of about twenty years by the house's sheet, at about 17 to 18 per cent alcohol.
wine.glass: Dark olive brown with a green tinge at the rim; raisin and Christmas pudding with a sweetly spiced edge over soft woody notes, intensely sweet and thick, the old reserves giving depth and the younger wine a fresh lift of grape.

records.table: Very old reserves of Brown Muscat, blended with younger wine to an average of about twenty years, make the Old Premium Rare Liqueur Muscat of Morris of Rutherglen: raisin and Christmas pudding with a sweetly spiced edge, thick and long. records.story: George Francis Morris (1834 to 1910) bought land near Rutherglen at auction in 1859 and, by the house's account, planted a trial vineyard that year at Fairfield, two miles east of the later winery. In the early 1860s he built a house called Fairfield with his first cellar beneath its ballroom, and he went on to buy land across the district. In the late 1890s phylloxera crippled Rutherglen's vineyards. In 1897 his son planted a new vineyard at Mia Mia, a few kilometres away, selling the family's prize horse, Fairfield, to pay for it, and a horse became the company's emblem. The family sold the business around 1970; it passed through company hands, Pernod Ricard's among them from 1989, and in 2016 Casella Family Brands, itself a family company, bought it from Pernod Ricard. Through those years the reserve casks went on growing older, and the Old Premium range is drawn from them. Whoever owned it, the Morris name has stayed on the gate since 1859, and in the glass it is Rutherglen Muscat on its sweet, thick and opulent side.

wine.serve: Lightly chilled, 10 to 13 degrees Celsius, cooler in summer; no decanting; a small white wine glass, after dinner with coffee or blue cheese.

records.table: A ship gave Campbells' Rare Rutherglen Muscat its name, the Merchant Prince that brought the founder from Scotland: Brown Muscat aged in solera to an average of over fifty years, by the house's account, with raisin, walnut and a long, drying finish.
records.story: In 1857 a young Scot sailed for Australia from St Andrews aboard the Merchant Prince, as the family tells it, and by its account he reached Rutherglen in 1860 to dig for gold and worked the rich Bobbie Burns lead west of the township, then left the diggings for vines on the advice of the district's first winegrowers, and made his first vintage in 1870. After phylloxera his son replanted the vineyards on American rootstock, with his wife's help, by the house's account, and the house later gave her name, Isabella, to its Rare Tokay. The family's Muscats and Topaques age in soleras, many holding the wines of four generations. The house launched Merchant Prince, its Rare Muscat, in 1983, and Isabella followed in 1990; when Tokay left Australian labels under the agreement of 2008 with the European Union, Isabella became a Topaque. The Bobbie Burns Shiraz, named for the gold lead, reached its thirtieth consecutive vintage in 1999. Known at once for a dry red and for its Rare Muscat, Campbells puts on the Muscat's label a ship that carries the family's beginning to the table.

records.table: In the castle built winery at Wahgunyah, on the Murray, All Saints Estate blends old reserves of Brown Muscat to an average of about forty five years for its Rare Rutherglen Muscat, which tastes of fig, burnt orange and baked apple. It wants small glasses and a light chill.
records.story: Two friends from Caithness, in the far north of Scotland, began growing vines at Wahgunyah on the Murray River in 1864, by the estate's account. They built a winery that recalls the Castle of Mey in their home county, with turrets and a tower, though the estate itself says only the battlements and the turrets were copied; the building is listed on the Victorian Heritage Register. By the estate's account its wine won a gold medal in London in 1873. Inside, the Great Hall is lined with old oak casks of Muscat and Tokay. In the 1990s the estate passed to the Brown family of Milawa, the makers of Brown Brothers, and after the sudden death in 2005 of the family member who had owned it, it passed to his children. The estate's oldest stocks, more than a century old, go into a Museum Muscat filled to order in very small numbers; the Rare is the house's wine at the fourth rung of the Rutherglen ladder, above Grand. At All Saints the district's past can be seen as well as tasted: a Scottish castle on the Murray, and Muscat drawn from its old casks.

wine.name: Vintage Fortified
wine.grapes: Portuguese grapes, Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca and Tinta Cão, with Shiraz and Durif; the mix changes from year to year.
wine.sites: The family's Rutherglen vineyards, where Portuguese varieties were planted through the 1980s and 1990s beside the district's Shiraz and Durif.
wine.making: Each wine is of one year: the red grapes are fermented and fortified with spirit distilled from grape material, then held for about twelve months before bottling, by the house's account. It then ages in bottle. The style aims at a drier, firmer wine than the big, sweet Australian vintage fortified of the past.
wine.glass: Young, it shows dried fig, red cherry, caramel and vanilla over firm tannin and the warmth of spirit; with age it turns to raisin, Christmas cake and a rancio edge, drier than most Australian fortified reds.
wine.ageing: Firm when released, it repays ten to twenty years in bottle, and the house gives its vintage wines thirty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, as for vintage Port; stand an older bottle upright, then decant it off its sediment; a small wine glass.

records.table: Touriga Nacional and other Portuguese grapes meet Shiraz and Durif in Stanton & Killeen's Vintage Fortified, a Rutherglen red of a single year made in the manner of vintage Port, drier and firmer than the old Australian style. Lay it down for years, then decant it.
records.story: The Stanton family came from Suffolk, by its own account, and around 1864 a father and son bought land at Rutherglen and supplied fortified wine to the miners of the goldfields. In 1875 they made their first official vintage, as Stanton Wines, in a red gum slab winery at Bank Hill. Phylloxera, drought and the Depression all tested the family in turn. A Killeen married a Stanton daughter, and in 1968 the business took the name Stanton and Killeen Wines. Through the 1980s and 1990s the sixth generation winemaker, who died in 2007, planted Portuguese varieties, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Touriga and Tinta Cão, to make his own Australian vintage fortified, finer and drier than the sweet style of the district's past. The wine was sold for years as Vintage Port, until the wine agreements with the European Union closed the word to Australian makers and Vintage Fortified became its name. The house makes Muscat and Topaque too, yet in Rutherglen its name is tied to a fortified red of one year, the district's answer to the Douro.
